text:
The chair had been on the curb two days before I met the couple.

It faced the wrong way, the way things do when someone drags them out and stops caring how the world reads them. One armrest was blackened to a glassy sheen, the wood warped into a curl like a burnt fingernail. The front legs were scorched pale, and even in the October wind the smell clung to it, faint, sweet, unmistakable. Fire is a confession. People who burn things want someone to know.

That evening I was already in the mood for ruins when I saw them walking south on Meridian as the rain began. The man wore a work jacket with a faded patch and a cap pulled low. The woman carried a paper grocery bag and, under her other arm, a small cardboard box. They argued gently, the way married people argue when the argument is mostly about the weather.

"The plumber said Thursday," the woman said. "He said Thursday, and it's Thursday."

"Maybe he's stuck on the highway," the man said. "It's raining like it's trying to drown the state."

She laughed, short and practical, and adjusted the box twice, shifting her weight to her left leg, and her right shoe was brown and her left was black, dressed in a hurry, chosen without looking. It's the mismatched shoe that stops a man walking, that says here is a person, assembled imperfectly out of whatever she had on hand.

They turned a side street and kept going, and I kept going behind them. I want to be honest about that. I told myself I was testing the streetlights, which were being replaced that week, which is true, and which is also the kind of thing a man says to himself at ten o'clock at night, standing in a doorway looking through a kitchen window.

Their house sat at the end of a lane below the grade of everything else, the block that floods first and freezes last. I had walked it years ago, apartment hunting; the woman at the office had called it "a bit low," "pools in storms." Now I stood across the street with my hands in my pockets and looked through the kitchen window, where a porch light made their shapes clear against the wet dark.

And there, propped by the back door, armrest blackened, legs scorched pale, was the chair.

I knew the curl on that wood the way you know a face from a photograph taken forty years ago. Someone had gone back for it, driven past or walked past, taken it home, put it up where it would be easy to see.

The rain thickened. By six the water was finding its way downhill, and downhill there meant the lane. The sump pump in the next house cycled on and off like a tired animal. Neighbors came out with buckets and tarps, standing to the tops of their boots, laughing at it.

I watched from the curb above, where the water had only reached the gutter. My own street was flooding too. I stayed, because there was something I needed to see, though I couldn't have named it.

The couple came out around seven. The man first, porch light in one hand, laundry basket in the other, stepping through the water with the annoyed economy of a man who has dealt with weather all his life and considers it an insult. Then the woman, barefoot in socks, carrying the chair.

She carried it the way you carry a chair you've carried a hundred times, by the seat, the burned armrest angled toward the street, and set it at the threshold, facing the water. The flood had already come under the door, ankle-deep and gray, carrying a plastic bag and a bottle cap. She sat down.

She sat down and put her hands in her lap, and the water came up over her socks, and she did not move.

The man stood behind her with the light, then set the laundry basket on the step, and then, without any of it looking like a decision, sat beside her, boots taking the water, cap still on, holding the light over them like a reading lamp.

I stood on the curb and felt the cold come through my shoes, and I understood at last what I'd been circling for two days. Whatever had been burned with that chair had been burned on purpose. She had carried the burned thing home instead of leaving it for the garbage truck, and she had waited. She set the chair out where the water would find it and sat in it the way a person sits in a chair she has sat in a thousand times, whole weight settled, unhurried. She had discarded nothing. She had set it out like a plate on a table, waiting for the world to come down and take her back.

I think about how much of my life I've spent doing the opposite, standing over ruined things and walking past, following other people's ruined things around the block, hoping someone would show me what to do with mine.

The man said something low. She answered. Their voices were small and ordinary over the water, about the plumber, about Thursday, about whether the power would hold. Nothing about the chair. Nothing about the water except as weather, as inconvenience.

At midnight the sirens stopped, which is how you know a flood is over in a city. I went home then, through streets turned into rivers with sidewalks in them, climbed my own stairs, unlocked my own door. The water was there too, of course, because everything was low, because everything was where the rain lands.

I stood in my own kitchen in my own socks and looked around for something to sit in, and I had nothing. Not a chair, not even a burned one. Years ago I had burned something of mine over a kitchen stove, slowly, the way you burn letters, the things that would identify you to a stranger if they were found. I carried the ashes to the curb in a tin can, tipped them into the gutter, and walked away. Never once thought to go back and collect whatever was left.

I sat on my kitchen floor instead, in the dark, in the water, listening to the pump in the wall cycle on and off. She went back for hers.

The water reached my boots around three in the morning. I did not go to the step. I stayed on the floor with nothing to sit in and let it rise the way it rose.
